paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: The photoelectric effect is the release of electrons from a material when electromagnetic radiation, such as ultraviolet light, falls on it. The electrons that come out are called photoelectrons. Researchers use the effect to learn about the properties of atoms, molecules and solids. It is also built into electronic devices that detect light or release electrons at precisely timed moments.

paragraphs.heading: The puzzle
paragraphs.text: Classical electromagnetism expected light to act as a continuous wave, feeding energy into electrons until they had enough to escape. On that view, changing the brightness of the light should change the energy of the emitted electrons, and very dim light should simply take longer to work. Experiments showed something else. Electrons come out only when the light's frequency is above a certain value, no matter how bright the light is or how long it shines.

paragraphs.heading: Einstein's packets of light
paragraphs.text: Albert Einstein suggested that light is not a wave spreading through space but a stream of separate packets of energy, later called photons. Each photon carries an energy, called the photon energy, in proportion to the light's frequency. Making low-frequency light brighter only adds more low-energy photons, and none of them alone can free an electron. Likewise, the energy of the emitted electrons depends only on the energy of single photons, not on the light's intensity. Work on the effect was an important step toward seeing the quantum nature of light and electrons, and it helped shape the idea of wave–particle duality.

paragraphs.heading: All or nothing
paragraphs.text: Inside a material, an electron that absorbs a photon and gains more energy than its binding energy is likely to be thrown out. If the photon energy is too low, the electron cannot escape. In quantum systems, an electron takes in all of one photon's energy or none of it. Part of that energy frees the electron from its atom, and the rest becomes its kinetic energy as a free particle.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the energy
paragraphs.text: The classic setup uses filtered light, a vacuum tube, an emitting electrode that the light strikes, and a collector whose voltage can be adjusted. A positive voltage draws the photoelectrons onto the collector. A growing negative voltage instead turns back all but the highest-energy electrons. The voltage at which the current stops entirely is called the stopping potential, Vₒ. It reveals the largest kinetic energy of the electrons through eVₒ = Kₘₐₓ, where e is the electron's charge.

paragraphs.heading: The threshold
paragraphs.text: Every metal surface has a threshold frequency, below which no photoelectrons are emitted at all. Raising the frequency increases the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, so the stopping voltage must rise too. For typical metals, freeing conduction electrons needs light quanta of a few electron-volts, which means short-wavelength visible or ultraviolet light. Oxide layers on metal usually raise the barrier to emission, so most experiments and devices use clean metal surfaces in evacuated tubes.
